full_judgment:
7. This Court notes at the outset the submission of the Learned Counsel for the petitioner, Md Muzibur Rahman that keeping in view the necessity to consider in their entirety the facts and evidence as were before the courts below, the essential starting point must be the fact of execution and registration of the Kabala dated 5-1-1991. In this regard, it is this Court's view that certain presumptions of law and rules of pleading must be taken into account before a court can delve into specific issues of fact and evidence. Rules of pleadings are significant here in light of allegations of fraud, deceit and collusion made by the plaintiff-opposite party. 

 8. It is evident to this Court that the Kabala dated 5-1-1991 represents a registered deed, the registration of which was proven in the statements of the DW 2, DW 4, DW 5 identifiers and DW 3 scribe of the deed to the satisfaction of the trial Court. The act of registration as arises under section 60 of The Registration Act, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') and evident in the issuance of a certificate of registration, is premised, as evident in section 60 itself, upon an extensive process of enquiry, admission and denial of execution, as well as of admission to registration as stipulated in sections 34, 35, 38 and 59 of the Act. This, therefore, raises the presumption of law that at the very least the registration process itself was regular and honestly carried out. As observed in Gangamoyi Debi vs Troiluckhya Nath Chowdhury and another reported in 33 lA 60 at 65: 

 9. This presumption as observed by the Appellate Division in Abani Mohan Saha vs Assistant Custodian (SDO) Vested Property, Chandpur and ors reported in 39 DLR (AD) 223 strongly attests to the genuineness of registered documents under section 60 of the Act. Indeed, and as was also the case in the Gangamoyi Debi Case, the matter before us also involved the element of an alleged deliberate fraud and collusion committed, an allegation that necessarily must be substantiated under stringent rules of proof and scrutiny. Of course, by virtue of Proviso 1 of section 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872 oral evidence may be admitted to contradict, vary or subtract from any terms of a contract or other disposition of property reduced to the form of a document, it is nevertheless the case by reason of rules of pleadings developed by judicial authority that allegations of deceit, fraud and collusion have to be brought and framed in a particular manner. Read with Order VI, rule 4 of the Code such judicial authority stresses that general allegations, however strong the words, are insufficient to substantiate an averment of fraud. In other words, what is required are positive statements and affirmations coupled with the offer of strong and substantial evidence. That apparently is the line of reasoning adopted by the learned Senior Assistant Judge-in-Charge when considering the crucial aspect of fraud and collusion ostensibly leading to the plaintiff-opposite party affixing her left thumb impression (LTI) in execution of the Kabala. Finding that no credible or substantial evidence had been adduced by or on behalf of the plaintiff either to show and prove the nature and extent of her claimed ailment at the time, and the manner in which she may have been induced to affix her LTI several times on the Kabala in question, the trial Court came to a finding that the burden of proof required of the plaintiff-opposite party in discharge of her responsibility to prove fraud and collusion had not been so done sufficiently in keeping with standards established in long-standing judicial authority. It is in that context this Court has taken note of the reference in the trial Court's judgment to the observation on the standard of discharging the onus of proof in such circumstances as found in the case of Kiron Chandra Das vs Sirajul Hoque Patwari reported in 34 DLR 225 at paragraph 5, 226 thus: 

 "There is a presumption of good faith in human transaction as there is a presumption of innocence in criminal matters. That being so the burden of proving every species of bad faith such as fraud, collusion, misrepresentation, impersonation, undue influence, absence of consideration rests on the person who asserts the same and only after that burden was discharged prima facie the burden would shift on the other party to prove that it was not so." 

 11. It is at this juncture that the trial Court took note of, and duly considered, the weight in balance of the evidence given by the DWs 2, 3, 4 and 5 all identifiers and scribe of the registered Kabala in proving the execution of the same. The learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioner Mr Rahman submits that while the trial Court appropriately gave its due weight in consideration to such evidence of execution as adduced by the DWs 2,3,4 and 5, the lower appellate Court ignored and/or misread the same to its peril. In this regard, Mr Rahman, has drawn this Court's attention to the Appellate Division's Judgment and order in Saheda Khatun (Most) & others vs Sheikh Md Ramjan Ali reported in 10 MLR (AD) 194. It is evident to this Court that the Learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioner relies on this case as it elaborates on his initial submission that in a case as this, the court has primarily to look into the consequence and presumption of law that automatically follows upon a deed shown to be registered. This Court has already considered the long line of established judicial authority that endorses the presumptions of due process of registration and of the consequential genuineness of execution unless effectively rebutted by strong evidence of fraud, collusion and deceit. This Court has already observed in agreement with the findings of the trial Court that rules of pleadings and standards essential to establish and prove fraud, deceit and collusion have not been satisfactorily adhered to by the plaintiff-opposite party in this case. This Court is also of the view that, and considering the preponderance of evidence considered by the trial Court, should the words 'fraud', 'deceit' and 'collusion' be taken away from the plaintiffs pleadings, one is necessarily left with obscure allegations of acts that do not necessarily appear to be tainted by illegality. 

 12. The Learned Counsel for the plaintiff-opposite party Ms Azra Ali submits that the Saheda Khatun case has no manner of application to the facts and circumstances of this case, chiefly because this case pertains to a registered sale deed whereas the judgment in the Saheda Khatun Case has been given in the context of a Heba deed. Mindful of such distinction, the Court, nevertheless, notes the similarity of issues between that case and this. As in this case so in the Saheda Khatun Case, the allegation was that LTI was obtained on a blank stamp-paper upon practising deception leading to the fabrication of a gift-deed. The Saheda Khatun Case was also one where it was found that the plaintiff's case was lacking in material evidence substantiating her allegations of fraud. It was found that the defendant having proven the genuineness of the execution and registration of the deed by examining the material evidence as given by the scribe, the attesting witness and the identifier, the courts below perfectly and justifiably dismissed the suit. This Court, in considering the above-referred judgment, finds itself in disagreement with Ms Azra Ail's submission that simply by reason of distinction as to the nature of the deed at issue the Saheda Khatun Case is of no manner of application here. On the contrary, this Court finds that the Appellate Division's judgment in that case strikes at the very core of this case and supports the finding that there being no effective rebuttal by the plaintiff-opposite party of the presumption of genuine execution and due registration of the Kabala dated 5-1-1991, then given the general and unsubstantiated allegations of fraud and collusion, the trial Court, upon a consideration of all material evidence, was correct in dismissing the plaintiff's suit.
